passage:
Age two: Ojas cried at the door when his father put him down to make tea. He lifted both arms, and his father scooped him up again. Held against the chest, his breathing slowed. His father made the tea one-handed and said, 'Held is not spoiled.'

Age fifteen: Gautam stiffened when his aunt reached for a hug at the family dinner. He edged back, said 'Hi,' and sat at the far end. Later he came and sat beside her on the sofa, shoulder just touching hers, watching television. She said nothing about it and only shifted so he could lean. At bedtime his mother patted his back in passing, and he let her.

Age twenty-five: Omkar had lived alone in a new city for two months. He felt restless, snapped at a delivery driver and found himself lingering at the barber. He noticed the thought: when did anyone last hug me? He rang his sister, then went to a friend's flat for dinner and got a hug at the door. That night he slept better.

qa.q: What did Ojas's father say about holding?
How does the need for touch look at two, fifteen and twenty-five?
qa.a: Ojas asked to be picked up and calmed when held. Gautam stiffened at a family hug yet still leaned near his aunt on his own terms, and Omkar, alone in a new city, felt restless and sensitive until a hug and dinner with a friend.

qa.q: What was Gautam probably feeling when he sat beside his aunt with his shoulder touching hers?
qa.a: Still wanting warmth and closeness, even though he needed to set his own pace.

qa.q: How did Gautam's aunt keep the connection alive?
qa.a: She said nothing and only shifted so he could lean, respecting his pace.

grounding: Comfort through touch at two, fifteen and twenty-five: a toddler needing closeness, a teen pulling away yet craving warmth, and an isolated adult craving contact.
